events.truth_text: the father has remarried a proud and haughty woman
her two daughters prove as haughty as their mother

the two sisters are overjoyed and think of nothing but what to wear
Cinderella is expected to help them dress but is not imagined as a guest herself

the sisters jeer that it would make people laugh to see a Cinderwench at a ball
Cinderella does not ask to go
the stepmother and sisters depart for the ball
left alone, Cinderella weeps
the godmother appears and asks why Cinderella weeps
a pumpkin is turned into a golden coach; six mice into horses; a rat into a coachman; six lizards into footmen
Cinderella's rags become a gown of gold and silver, beset with jewels, and a pair of glass slippers
the godmother warns her in plain terms: if she stays one moment past midnight, coach, horses, footmen, and gown will all revert
a hush falls and the dancing stops as she enters
the old King himself remarks on her beauty
the King's son leads her out to dance
no one — including her own stepmother and sisters — recognizes her
Cinderella sits with her sisters and shares the oranges and citrons the Prince gave her
the sisters do not know her
she leaves at a quarter to twelve, well ahead of the deadline, and thanks the King and the Prince for their civility
she reaches home safely, with time to spare
Cinderella thanks her godmother
she confesses she would be glad to go to the ball again the next night
the godmother agrees to send her again
the sisters return home and can talk of nothing but the beautiful unknown princess at the ball
Cinderella asks the princess's name; the sisters say they do not know it
Cinderella asks, with feigned idle curiosity, to borrow Miss Charlotte's yellow suit so she might see the ball for herself
she is refused and mocked for the suggestion, as expected
Cinderella returns for the second ball, more beautifully dressed than before
she is so happy she loses all track of time
she hears the clock begin to strike twelve and flees the hall at once
in her haste she loses one glass slipper on the palace steps
the Prince picks up the slipper she left behind, having failed to catch her
at the last stroke of midnight, coach, horses, coachman, footmen, and gown all revert to a pumpkin, mice, a rat, lizards, and rags
Cinderella arrives home on foot, in her old clothes, out of breath
of all her finery, only the fellow glass slipper remains, kept in her pocket
she says nothing of the ball to anyone in the household
the Prince has it proclaimed by trumpet that he will marry whichever lady's foot fits the glass slipper
the slipper is tried on princesses, then duchesses, then all the ladies of the court, in vain
the search reaches at last the house of Cinderella's father
the sisters try the slipper in vain, squeezing and forcing their feet
Cinderella asks if she may try, and is laughed at
the gentleman-in-waiting says he has orders to let every maiden try, and looks earnestly at Cinderella, finding her very beautiful
the slipper goes onto her foot with perfect ease
Cinderella draws the fellow slipper from her pocket and puts it on
the godmother appears and touches Cinderella's clothes with her wand, turning them richer than ever before, in full view of the sisters this time
the two sisters fling themselves at Cinderella's feet and beg pardon for all their ill usage of her
Cinderella forgives them freely and embraces them, and says she loves them with all her heart
she is taken to the palace and presented to the Prince, lovelier than ever
they are married within a few days
Cinderella, as good as she is beautiful, lodges her sisters in the palace and that same day marries them to two great lords of the court
